lead: A segmented region is a blob of pixels. Its boundary is the ordered line around it. Walk that line and write a direction number at every step; the boundary becomes a short string such as 00664422. That string is a chain code. It saves memory, makes matching cheap, and gives numbers for length, turns and shape. Scanners, defect inspection and shape sorting use it. The same object can start at a different boundary pixel or be rotated, so the raw string is normalised into a first difference and a shape number.
prereq: You need boundary linking from 4.3 and pixel connectivity from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Following the boundary and writing a chain code

blocks.text: Segmentation gives a set of region pixels. To get an ordered boundary, pick a start pixel, for example the topmost row and then the leftmost pixel in that row. Move around the region clockwise. At each step choose the next boundary pixel by a fixed neighbour order. Stop when you return to the start. The output is a list of boundary coordinates in order.

Instead of storing coordinates, store the direction from one boundary pixel to the next. In a 4-directional code the directions are 0 = east, 1 = north, 2 = west, 3 = south. In the 8-directional Freeman code the directions are 0 = east, 1 = north-east, 2 = north, 3 = north-west, 4 = west, 5 = south-west, 6 = south, 7 = south-east. Image rows run downwards, so north is one row up and south is one row down. Each code is one step to a neighbour.

items: Find the start: topmost boundary pixel, then leftmost in that row.
Set the current pixel to the start. At the first step, set the previous point to the outside neighbour above-left of the start pixel.
Scan the eight neighbours of the current pixel clockwise starting from the previous point, skip the previous point itself, and take the first neighbour that belongs to the region.
Append the direction code to that neighbour. Set the previous point to the current pixel and make the chosen neighbour the new current pixel.
Stop when the start is reached again after at least one step.

blocks.text: A 4-directional code can only turn in right angles. A diagonal edge needs the 8-directional code. An N-pixel boundary needs N codes; in 8-direction each code fits in 3 bits.

sections.h3: Start point, first difference and shape number

blocks.text: The raw chain code depends on the start pixel, on the tracing direction and on rotation. The first difference removes rotations by multiples of 45 degrees, and the shape number removes the start pixel. Tracing direction is not removed, so always trace in the same direction (here clockwise) before comparing shape numbers.
d<sub>i</sub> = (a<sub>i</sub> − a<sub>i−1</sub>) mod 8, with a<sub>−1</sub> = a<sub>n−1</sub>
blocks.where: a<sub>i</sub> is the i-th chain code (0 to 7), n is the number of codes, and mod 8 keeps the result in 0 to 7. The first difference d<sub>i</sub> is the turn at step i.

blocks.text: Use the last code as the code before the first. A rotation by a multiple of 45° adds the same constant to every a<sub>i</sub>; the subtraction cancels it, so the first difference does not change. The shape number is the smallest circular rotation of the first difference, comparing digit by digit. It removes the start point. It does not remove scale.

Resampling on a coarser grid changes the number of codes. Before comparing shapes, resample the boundary on a fixed grid spacing. Conventionally the resampling is done so that the number of codes is a power of 2 (8, 16, 32, ...), which keeps the grid square and makes the 45 degree rotations consistent. The figure uses a 3×3 ring. Its clockwise code is 0 0 6 6 4 4 2 2. The first difference is 6 0 6 0 6 0 6 0. Rotating it once gives 0 6 0 6 0 6 0 6, the smallest rotation, so the shape number is 06060606.

sections.h3: Boundary descriptors: length, shape and Fourier coefficients

blocks.text: Several numbers summarise a boundary without keeping every pixel.

items: Boundary length from the code: L = N<sub>e</sub> + √2 N<sub>o</sub>. N<sub>e</sub> counts even codes 0, 2, 4, 6: each is a unit horizontal or vertical step. N<sub>o</sub> counts odd codes 1, 3, 5, 7: each is a diagonal step of length √2. L is in pixel units.
Diameter: the largest Euclidean distance between any two boundary points.
Eccentricity: major axis length ÷ minor axis length of the best-fitting ellipse. A circle has eccentricity 1; a long shape has a large value.

Curvature: rate of change of the tangent direction with arc length. For a first difference d, read d as a signed turn: 0, 1, 2, 3 are left turns of 0, 45, 90, 135 degrees, and 5, 6, 7 are right turns of 135, 90, 45 degrees; 4 is a full reversal. The size of the bend is min(d, 8 − d) × 45 degrees, so 7 and 1 are gentle turns and 4 is the sharpest.

blocks.text: z(k) = x(k) + j y(k); Z(u) = Σ<sub>k=0</sub><sup>N−1</sup> z(k) e<sup>−j2πuk/N</sup>
blocks.where: x(k), y(k) are the coordinates of boundary point k, N is the number of points, j is the imaginary unit, u is the frequency index, and Z(u) is the DFT coefficient.

blocks.text: Keep only the first few Z(u), usually the low frequencies. They describe the overall shape; high frequencies describe fine detail. Except Z(0), the magnitudes |Z(u)| do not change under translation, rotation or a change of start point. Scaling multiplies every magnitude by the same factor, so divide by |Z(1)| to compare sizes. Skeletons are a regional descriptor and are covered in 4.9.

spec.aria: A 3 by 3 ring of pixels with an empty centre and arrows around the boundary labelled 0, 0, 6, 6, 4, 4, 2, 2. A compass shows the eight Freeman directions 0 to 7. Three rows give the chain code, first difference and shape number.

examples.question: A 3×3 region has all pixels on except the centre. Use the outer boundary only. Trace it clockwise starting at the top-left pixel (0,0), with coordinates written as (row, column). Use the 8-directional Freeman code with rows increasing downwards. (a) Write the chain code. (b) Find the first difference. (c) Find the shape number. (d) Find the boundary length from the code.
steps: Start at (0,0). The boundary pixels in clockwise order are (0,0), (0,1), (0,2), (1,2), (2,2), (2,1), (2,0), (1,0), and back to (0,0).
Circular rotations include 60606060 and 06060606. The smallest starts with 0, so shape number = 0 6 0 6 0 6 0 6.
All 8 codes are even: N<sub>e</sub> = 8. No code is odd: N<sub>o</sub> = 0. L = 8 + √2·0 = 8 pixels.
examples.answer: Chain code 0 0 6 6 4 4 2 2; first difference 6 0 6 0 6 0 6 0; shape number 0 6 0 6 0 6 0 6; boundary length L = 8 pixels with N<sub>e</sub> = 8 and N<sub>o</sub> = 0.
examples.check:
import math
pts = [(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,2),(2,2),(2,1),(2,0),(1,0)]
code = []
for (r1,c1),(r2,c2) in zip(pts, pts[1:]+pts[:1]):
    dr = r2 - r1
    dc = c2 - c1
    if dr == 0 and dc == 1:
        code.append(0)
    elif dr == -1 and dc == 1:
        code.append(1)
    elif dr == -1 and dc == 0:
        code.append(2)
    elif dr == -1 and dc == -1:
        code.append(3)
    elif dr == 0 and dc == -1:
        code.append(4)
    elif dr == 1 and dc == -1:
        code.append(5)
    elif dr == 1 and dc == 0:
        code.append(6)
    elif dr == 1 and dc == 1:
        code.append(7)
    else:
        raise ValueError('not a neighbour step')
assert code == [0,0,6,6,4,4,2,2]
diff = [(code[i] - code[i-1]) % 8 for i in range(len(code))]
assert diff == [6,0,6,0,6,0,6,0]
rots = [diff[i:]+diff[:i] for i in range(len(diff))]
shape = min(rots)
assert shape == [0,6,0,6,0,6,0,6]
Ne = sum(1 for x in code if x in (0,2,4,6))
No = len(code) - Ne
L = Ne + math.sqrt(2) * No
print(int(L))
print(Ne)
print(No)

traps: The first difference must be taken mod 8. Writing −2 instead of 6 for a step from 4 to 2 breaks the shape number.
The raw chain code depends on the start pixel and on clockwise versus anticlockwise tracing. State both when you give a raw code.
4-directional and 8-directional codes use different meanings for the same number. In a 4-code 1 means north; in an 8-code 1 means north-east.
Boundary length is not just the number of codes for an 8-directional boundary. Odd codes are diagonal steps of length √2, not 1.
The shape number is the smallest circular rotation of the first difference, not of the raw chain code.

quiz.q: In the 8-directional Freeman code, what direction does code 6 mean when image rows increase downwards?
quiz.a: South: one pixel down, same column.

quiz.q: Why does taking the first difference remove the effect of rotating the whole object by 45°?
quiz.a: A 45° rotation adds the same constant k modulo 8 to every chain code. Each difference (a<sub>i</sub> − a<sub>i−1</sub>) cancels k, so the difference string is unchanged.

quiz.q: A boundary has chain code 0 1 0 1. Find the first difference with a<sub>−1</sub> = 1, then find the shape number.
quiz.a: Differences: (0−1) mod 8 = 7; (1−0) = 1; (0−1) mod 8 = 7; (1−0) = 1. First difference = 7 1 7 1. Rotations are 7171 and 1717; the smallest is 1717, so the shape number is 1717.

quiz.q: An 8-directional chain code has 10 even codes and 6 odd codes. Find the boundary length in pixel units.
Two boundaries have the same shape number but different sizes. What does that tell you?
quiz.a: They have the same start-normalised turning pattern, so their shapes are similar. The shape number does not encode scale, so the actual sizes can differ.

quiz.q: Why does keeping only low-frequency Fourier descriptors compress a shape while still allowing matching?
quiz.a: Low frequencies carry the overall outline; high frequencies carry fine detail. Dropping high coefficients reduces data and smooths small variations, while the kept coefficients still separate broad shape classes.

quiz.q: Write the boundary length formula for an 8-directional chain code.
quiz.a: L = N<sub>e</sub> + √2 N<sub>o</sub>, where N<sub>e</sub> counts codes 0, 2, 4, 6 and N<sub>o</sub> counts codes 1, 3, 5, 7.

quiz.q: Why is a raw chain code not directly used to compare two identical objects that start at different boundary pixels?
quiz.a: Starting at a different pixel circularly shifts the code. The same boundary then gives a different string. The shape number or a comparison over all rotations removes this shift.

beyond: Not for the exam. Chain codes are still used in embedded vision because they are tiny: a 1000-pixel boundary costs about 3 kbits in an 8-directional code. Modern shape retrieval often uses Fourier descriptors or learned embeddings, but the same normalisation ideas apply. Search for Freeman chain code, shape number and Fourier descriptors. In robotics, chain codes help represent obstacle outlines for grid path planning.
